them. As long as they’ve got her, they’ve got the whip hand of us. See?”"}, {"paragraph": 120, "text": "“Sure thing,” said Julius thoughtfully. “That’s so.”"}, {"paragraph": 121, "text": "“Besides,” added Tommy, as an afterthought, “I’ve great faith in
Tuppence.”"}, {"paragraph": 122, "text": "The journey was wearisome, with many stops, and crowded carriages. They
had to change twice, once at Doncaster, once at a small junction. Ebury
was a deserted station with a solitary porter, to whom Tommy addressed
himself:"}, {"paragraph": 123, "text": "“Can you tell me the way to the Moat House?”"}, {"paragraph": 124, "text": "“The Moat House? It’s a tidy step from here. The big house near the sea,
you mean?”"}, {"paragraph": 125, "text": "Tommy assented brazenly. After listening to the porter’s meticulous
but perplexing directions, they prepared to leave the station. It was
beginning to rain, and they turned up the collars of their coats as they
trudged through the slush of the road. Suddenly Tommy halted."}, {"paragraph": 126, "text": "“Wait a moment.” He ran back to the station and tackled the porter anew."}, {"paragraph": 127, "text": "“Look here, do you remember a young lady who arrived by an earlier
train, the 12.50 from London? She’d probably ask you the way to the Moat
House.”"}, {"paragraph": 128, "text": "He described Tuppence as well as he could, but the porter shook his
head. Several people had arrived by the train in question. He could not
call to mind one young lady in particular. But he was quite certain that
no one had asked him the way to the Moat House."}, {"paragraph": 129, "text": "Tommy rejoined Julius, and explained. Depression was settling on him
like a leaden weight. He felt convinced that their quest was going to
be unsuccessful. The enemy had over three hours’ start. Three hours was
more than enough for Mr. Brown. He would not ignore the possibility of
the telegram having been found."}, {"paragraph": 130, "text": "The way seemed endless. Once they took the wrong turning and went nearly
half a mile out of their direction. It was past seven o’clock when a
small boy told them that “t’ Moat House” was just past the next corner."}, {"paragraph": 131, "text": "A rusty iron gate swinging dismally on its hinges! An overgrown drive
thick with leaves. There was something about the place that struck a
chill to both their hearts. They went up the deserted drive. The leaves
deadened their footsteps. The daylight was almost gone. It was like
walking in a world of ghosts. Overhead the branches flapped and creaked
with a mournful note. Occasionally a sodden leaf drifted silently down,
startling them with its cold touch on their cheek."}, {"paragraph": 132, "text": "A turn of the drive brought them in sight of the house. That, too,
seemed empty and deserted. The shutters were closed, the steps up to
the door overgrown with moss. Was it indeed to this desolate spot
that Tuppence had been decoyed? It seemed hard to believe that a human
footstep had passed this way for months."}, {"paragraph": 133, "text": "Julius jerked the rusty bell handle. A jangling peal rang discordantly,
echoing through the emptiness within. No one came. They rang again and
again--but there was no sign of life. Then they walked completely round
the house. Everywhere silence, and shuttered windows. If they could
believe the evidence of their eyes the place was empty."}, {"paragraph": 134, "text": "“Nothing doing,” said Julius."}, {"paragraph": 135, "text": "They retraced their steps slowly to the gate."}, {"paragraph": 136, "text": "“There must be a village handy,” continued the young American. “We’d
better make inquiries there. They’ll know something about the place, and
whether there’s been anyone there lately.”"}, {"paragraph": 137, "text": "“Yes, that’s not a bad idea.”"}, {"paragraph": 138, "text": "Proceeding up the road, they soon came to a little hamlet. On the
outskirts of it, they met a workman swinging his bag of tools, and Tommy
stopped him with a question."}, {"paragraph": 139, "text": "“The Moat House? It’s empty. Been empty for years. Mrs. Sweeny’s got the
key if you want to go over it--next to the post office.”"}, {"paragraph": 140, "text": "Tommy thanked him. They soon found the post office, which was also a
sweet and general fancy shop, and knocked at the door of the cottage
next to it. A clean, wholesome-looking woman opened it. She readily
produced the key of the Moat House."}, {"paragraph": 141, "text": "“Though I doubt if it’s the kind of place to suit you, sir. In a
terrible state of repair. Ceilings leaking and all. ‘Twould need a lot
of money spent on it.”"}, {"paragraph": 142, "text": "“Thanks,” said Tommy cheerily. “I dare say it’ll be a washout, but
houses are scarce nowadays.”"}, {"paragraph": 143, "text": "“That they are,” declared the woman heartily. “My daughter and
son-in-law have been looking for a decent cottage for I don’t know how
long. It’s all the war. Upset things terribly, it has. But excuse me,
sir, it’ll be too dark for you to see much of the house. Hadn’t you
better wait until to-morrow?”"}, {"paragraph": 144, "text": "“That’s all right. We’ll have a look around this evening, anyway. We’d
have been here before only we lost our way. What’s the best place to
stay at for the night round here?”"}, {"paragraph": 145, "text": "Mrs. Sweeny looked doubtful."}, {"paragraph": 146, "text": "“There’s the _Yorkshire Arms_, but it’s not much of a place for
gentlemen like you.”"}, {"paragraph": 147, "text": "“Oh, it will do very well. Thanks. By the way, you’ve not had a young
lady here asking for this key to-day?”"}, {"paragraph": 148, "text": "The woman shook her head."}, {"paragraph": 149, "text": "“No one’s been over the place for a long time.”"}, {"paragraph": 150, "text": "“Thanks very much.”"}, {"paragraph": 151, "text": "They retraced their steps to the Moat House. As the front door swung
back on its hinges, protesting loudly, Julius struck a match and
examined the floor carefully. Then he shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 152, "text": "“I’d swear no one’s passed this way. Look at the dust. Thick. Not a sign
of a footmark.”"}, {"paragraph": 153, "text": "They wandered round the deserted house. Everywhere the same tale. Thick
layers of dust apparently undisturbed."}, {"paragraph": 154, "text": "“This gets me,” said Julius. “I don’t believe Tuppence was ever in this
house.”"}, {"paragraph": 155, "text": "“She must have been.”"}, {"paragraph": 156, "text": "Julius shook his head without replying."}, {"paragraph": 157, "text": "“We’ll go over it again to-morrow,” said Tommy. “Perhaps we’ll see more
in the daylight.”"}, {"paragraph": 158, "text": "On the morrow they took up the search once more, and were reluctantly
forced to the conclusion that the house had not been invaded for some
considerable time. They might have left the village altogether but for
a fortunate discovery of Tommy’s. As they were retracing their steps to
the gate, he gave a sudden cry, and stooping, picked something up from
among the leaves, and held it out to Julius. It was a small gold brooch."}, {"paragraph": 159, "text": "“That’s Tuppence’s!”"}, {"paragraph": 160, "text": "“Are you sure?”"}, {"paragraph": 161, "text": "“Absolutely. I’ve often seen her wear it.”"}, {"paragraph": 162, "text": "Julius drew a deep breath."}, {"paragraph": 163, "text": "“I guess that settles it. She came as far as here, anyway. We’ll make
that pub our head-quarters, and raise hell round here until we find her.
Somebody _must_ have seen her.”"}, {"paragraph": 164, "text": "Forthwith the campaign began. Tommy and Julius worked separately and
together, but the result was the same. Nobody answering to Tuppence’s
description had been seen in the vicinity. They were baffled--but not
discouraged. Finally they altered their tactics. Tuppence had certainly
not remained long in the neighbourhood of the Moat House. That pointed
to her having been overcome and carried away in a car. They renewed
inquiries. Had anyone seen a car standing somewhere near the Moat House
that day? Again they met with no success."}, {"paragraph": 165, "text": "Julius wired to town for his own car, and they scoured the neighbourhood
daily with unflagging zeal. A grey limousine on which they had set high
hopes was traced to Harrogate, and turned out to be the property of a
highly respectable maiden lady!"}, {"paragraph": 166, "text": "Each day saw them set out on a new quest. Julius was like a hound on
the leash. He followed up the slenderest clue. Every car that had passed
through the village on the fateful day was tracked down. He forced his
way into country properties and submitted the owners of the motors to
a searching cross-examination. His apologies were as thorough as his
methods, and seldom failed in disarming the indignation of his victims;
but, as day succeeded day, they were no nearer to discovering Tuppence’s
whereabouts. So well had the abduction been planned that the girl seemed
literally to have vanished into thin air."}, {"paragraph": 167, "text": "And another preoccupation was weighing on Tommy’s mind."}, {"paragraph": 168, "text": "“Do you know how long we’ve been here?” he asked one morning as they
sat facing each other at breakfast. “A week! We’re no nearer to finding
Tuppence, _and next Sunday is the_ 29_th!_”"}, {"paragraph": 169, "text": "“Shucks!” said Julius thoughtfully. “I’d almost forgotten about the
29th. I’ve been thinking of nothing but Tuppence.”"}, {"paragraph": 170, "text": "“So have I. At least, I hadn’t forgotten about the 29th, but it didn’t
seem to matter a damn in comparison to finding Tuppence. But to-day’s
the 23rd, and time’s getting short. If we’re ever going to get hold of
her at all, we must do it before the 29th--her life won’t be worth an
hour’s purchase afterwards. The hostage game will be played out by then.
I’m beginning to feel that we’ve made a big mistake in the way we’ve set
about this. We’ve wasted time and we’re no forrader.”"}, {"paragraph": 171, "text": "“I’m with you there. We’ve been a couple of mutts, who’ve bitten off a
bigger bit than they can chew. I’m going to quit fooling right away!”"}, {"paragraph": 172, "text": "“What do you mean?”"}, {"paragraph": 173, "text": "“I’ll tell you. I’m going to do what we ought to have done a week ago.
I’m going right back to London to put the case in the hands of your
British police. We fancied ourselves as sleuths. Sleuths! It was a piece
of damn-fool foolishness! I’m through! I’ve had enough of it. Scotland
Yard for me!”"}, {"paragraph": 174, "text": "“You’re right,” said Tommy slowly. “I wish to God we’d gone there right
away.”"}, {"paragraph": 175, "text": "“Better late than never. We’ve been like a couple of babes playing ‘Here
we go round the Mulberry Bush.’ Now I’m going right along to Scotland
Yard to ask them to take me by the hand and show me the way I should go.
I guess the professional always scores over the amateur in the end. Are
you coming along with me?”"}, {"paragraph": 176, "text": "Tommy shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 177, "text": "“What’s the good? One of us is enough. I might as well stay here and
nose round a bit longer. Something _might_ turn up. One never knows.”"}, {"paragraph": 178, "text": "“Sure thing. Well, so long. I’ll be back in a couple of shakes with a
few inspectors along. I shall tell them to pick out their brightest and
best.”"}, {"paragraph": 179, "text": "But the course of events was not to follow the plan Julius had laid
down. Later in the day Tommy received a wire:"}, {"paragraph": 180, "text": "“Join me Manchester Midland Hotel. Important news--JULIUS.”"}, {"paragraph": 181, "text": "At 7.30 that night Tommy alighted from a slow cross-country train.
Julius was on the platform."}, {"paragraph": 182, "text": "“Thought you’d come by this train if you weren’t out when my wire
arrived.”"}, {"paragraph": 183, "text": "Tommy grasped him by the arm."}, {"paragraph": 184, "text": "“What is it? Is Tuppence found?”"}, {"paragraph": 185, "text": "Julius shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 186, "text": "“No. But I found this waiting in London. Just arrived.”"}, {"paragraph": 187, "text": "He handed the telegraph form to the other. Tommy’s eyes opened as he
read:"}, {"paragraph": 188, "text": "“Jane Finn found. Come Manchester Midland Hotel immediately--PEEL
EDGERTON.”"}, {"paragraph": 189, "text": "Julius took the form back and folded it up."}, {"paragraph": 190, "text": "“Queer,” he said thoughtfully. “I thought that lawyer chap had quit!”"}], "019.revision": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "BAFFLED for the moment, Tommy strolled into the restaurant, and ordered a meal of surpassing excellence."}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "He was in the middle of conveying a particularly choice morsel of Sole à la Jeanette to his mouth, when he caught sight of Julius entering the room. Julius strode across, and pump-handled Tommy's hand with what seemed to the latter quite unnecessary vigour."}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": ""Holy snakes!" he ejaculated. "Is it really you?""}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": ""Of course it is. Why shouldn't it be?""}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": ""Why shouldn't it be? Say, man, don't you know you've been given up for dead?""}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": ""Who thought I was dead?" demanded Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": ""Tuppence.""}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": ""Where is Tuppence, by the way?" Tommy asked."}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": ""Isn't she here?""}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": ""No, the fellows at the office said she'd just gone out.""}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": ""Gone shopping, I guess. What on God's earth have you been doing all this time?""}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "Tommy plunged into his recital."}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "Julius listened spellbound."}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": ""Bully for you. Reads like a dime novel!""}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": ""And now for the home front," said Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "Julius, in his turn, assumed the rôle of narrator. Beginning with his unsuccessful reconnoitring at Bournemouth, he passed on to his return to London, the buying of the car, the growing anxieties of Tuppence, the call upon Sir James, and the sensational occurrences of the previous night."}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": ""But who killed her?" asked Tommy. "I don't quite understand.""}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": ""The doctor kidded himself she took it herself," replied Julius dryly."}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": ""And Sir James? What did he think?""}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": ""Being a legal luminary, he is likewise a human oyster," replied Julius. "I should say he 'reserved judgment.'" He went on to detail the events of the morning."}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": ""Lost her memory, eh?" said Tommy with interest. "By Jove, that explains why they looked at me so queerly when I spoke of questioning her.""}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": ""That bluff of yours was the goods all right," Julius said. "How you ever came to think of it all so pat beats me to a frazzle!""}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": ""I was in such a funk I had to think of something," said Tommy simply."}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "Tommy reverted to Mrs. Vandemeyer's death."}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": ""There's no doubt it was chloral?""}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": ""I believe not. But I guess Tuppence and I and even the highbrow Sir James have all got the same idea.""}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": ""Mr. Brown?" hazarded Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": ""Sure thing.""}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "Tommy nodded."}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": ""All the same," he said thoughtfully, "Mr. Brown hasn't got wings. I don't see how he got in and out.""}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": ""How about some high-class thought transference stunt?" Julius suggested. "Some magnetic influence that irresistibly impelled Mrs. Vandemeyer to commit suicide?""}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "Tommy looked at him with respect."}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": ""Good, Julius. Distinctly good. Especially the phraseology. But it leaves me cold. I yearn for a real Mr. Brown of flesh and blood.""}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "Inquiry at the office revealed the fact that Tuppence had not yet returned."}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": ""All the same, I guess I'll have a look round upstairs," said Julius. "She might be in my sitting-room." He disappeared."}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "Suddenly a diminutive boy spoke at Tommy's elbow:"}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": ""The young lady--she's gone away by train, I think, sir," he murmured shyly."}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": ""What?" Tommy wheeled round upon him."}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": ""The taxi, sir. I heard her tell the driver Charing Cross and to look sharp.""}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "Emboldened, the small boy proceeded. "So I thought, having asked for an A.B.C. and a Bradshaw.""}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": ""When did she ask for an A.B.C. and a Bradshaw?" Tommy interrupted."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": ""When I took her the telegram, sir. About half-past twelve.""}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": ""Tell me exactly what happened.""}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": ""I took up a telegram to No. 891--the lady was there. She opened it and gave a gasp, and then she said, very jolly like: 'Bring me up a Bradshaw, and an A.B.C., and look sharp, Henry.' My name isn't Henry, but----""}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": ""Never mind your name," said Tommy impatiently. "Go on.""}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": ""Yes, sir. I brought them, and she looked up something. And then 'Hurry up,' she says. 'Tell them to get me a taxi,' and she begins a-shoving on of her hat in front of the glass, and I seed her going into the taxi.""}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "At that moment Julius rejoined Tommy. He held an open letter in his hand."}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": ""I say, Hersheimmer"--Tommy turned to him--"Tuppence has gone off sleuthing on her own. She went off in a taxi to Charing Cross after getting a telegram." His eye fell on the letter in Julius's hand. "Oh; she left a note for you. That's all right. Where's she off to?""}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "Almost unconsciously, he held out his hand for the letter, but Julius folded it up and placed it in his pocket. He seemed a trifle embarrassed."}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": ""I guess this is nothing to do with it. It's about something else--something I asked her that she was to let me know about.""}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": ""Oh!" Tommy looked puzzled, and seemed waiting for more."}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": ""See here," said Julius suddenly, "I'd better put you wise. I asked Miss Tuppence to marry me this morning.""}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": ""Oh!" said Tommy mechanically. He felt dazed."}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": ""I'd like to tell you," continued Julius, "that before I suggested anything of the kind to Miss Tuppence, I made it clear that I didn't want to butt in in any way between her and you----""}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "Tommy roused himself."}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": ""That's all right," he said quickly. "Tuppence and I have been pals for years. Nothing more." He lit a cigarette with a hand that shook ever so little. "Tuppence always said that she was looking out for----""}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "He stopped abruptly, his face crimsoning, but Julius was in no way discomposed."}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": ""Oh, I guess it'll be the dollars that'll do the trick. Miss Tuppence put me wise to that right away. There's no humbug about her. We ought to gee along together very well.""}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "Tuppence and Julius! Well, why not? Had she not openly avowed her intention of marrying for money if she ever had the chance? Why blame her because she had been true to her creed?"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "Nevertheless, Tommy did blame her. He was filled with a passionate and utterly illogical resentment. It was all very well to _say_ things like that--but a _real_ girl would never marry for money. Tuppence was utterly cold-blooded and selfish, and he would be delighted if he never saw her again!"}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "Julius's voice broke in on these meditations."}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": ""Yes, we ought to gee along together very well. I've heard that a girl always refuses you once--a sort of convention.""}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "Tommy caught his arm."}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": ""Refuses? Did you say _refuses?_""}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": ""Sure thing. Didn't I tell you that? She just rapped out a 'no' without any kind of reason to it. But she'll come round right enough----""}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": ""What did she say in that note?" Tommy demanded fiercely."}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "The obliging Julius handed it to him."}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": ""There's no earthly clue in it as to where she's gone," he assured Tommy."}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "The note, in Tuppence's well-known schoolboy writing, ran as follows:"}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": ""DEAR JULIUS,"}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": ""It's always better to have things in black and white. I don't feel I can be bothered to think of marriage until Tommy is found. Let's leave it till then."}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": ""Yours affectionately,"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": ""TUPPENCE.""}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "Tommy handed it back, his eyes shining. He now felt that Tuppence was all that was noble and disinterested. Had she not refused Julius without hesitation? Darling Tuppence, there was not a girl in the world to touch her! When he saw her----His thoughts were brought up with a sudden jerk."}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": ""As you say," he remarked, pulling himself together, "there's not a hint here as to what she's up to. Hi--Henry!""}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "The small boy came obediently. Tommy produced five shillings."}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": ""Do you remember what the young lady did with the telegram?""}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": ""She crumpled it up into a ball and threw it into the grate, and made a sort of noise like 'Whoop!' sir," Henry said."}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": ""Very graphic, Henry," said Tommy. "Here's your five shillings. Come on, Julius. We must find that telegram.""}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "They hurried upstairs. In the fireplace was a crumpled ball of orange and white. Tommy disentangled it and smoothed out the telegram."}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": ""Come at once, Moat House, Ebury, Yorkshire, great developments--TOMMY.""}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "They looked at each other in stupefaction. Julius spoke first:"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": ""You didn't send it?""}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": ""Of course not. What does it mean?""}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": ""I guess it means the worst," said Julius quietly. "They've got her.""}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "_"What?"_"}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": ""Sure thing! They signed your name, and she fell into the trap like a lamb. But we've got to hustle. Where's that Bradshaw?""}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "After a few muttered imprecations Julius handed the Bradshaw to Tommy, who abandoned it in favour of an A.B.C."}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": ""Here we are. Ebury, Yorks. From King's Cross. (Boy must have made a mistake. It was King's Cross, not _Charing_ Cross.) 12.50, that's the train she went by. 2.10, that's gone. 3.20 is the next--and a damned slow train too. The great thing is to keep calm.""}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "Julius groaned."}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": ""That's so. But it gets my goat to think of that innocent young girl in danger!""}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "Tommy nodded abstractedly. He was thinking."}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": ""I say, Julius, what do they want her for, anyway? I don't think it's their game to do her any harm. She's a hostage, that's what she is. She's in no immediate danger, because if we tumble on to anything, she'd be damned useful to them. As long as they've got her, they've got the whip hand of us. See?""}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": ""Sure thing," said Julius thoughtfully. "That's so.""}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": ""Besides," added Tommy, as an afterthought, "I've great faith in Tuppence.""}, {"paragraph": 96, "text": "The journey was wearisome. Ebury was a deserted station with a solitary porter, to whom Tommy addressed himself:"}, {"paragraph": 97, "text": ""Look here, do you remember a young lady who arrived by an earlier train, the 12.50 from London? She'd probably ask you the way to the Moat House.""}, {"paragraph": 98, "text": "The porter shook his head. But he was quite certain that no one had asked him the way to the Moat House."}, {"paragraph": 99, "text": "It was past seven o'clock when a small boy told them that "t' Moat House" was just past the next corner."}, {"paragraph": 100, "text": "A rusty iron gate swinging dismally on its hinges! An overgrown drive thick with leaves. The house, too, seemed empty and deserted, the shutters closed, the steps overgrown with moss."}, {"paragraph": 101, "text": "Julius jerked the rusty bell handle. They rang again and again--but there was no sign of life."}, {"paragraph": 102, "text": ""Nothing doing," said Julius."}, {"paragraph": 103, "text": "On the outskirts of a little hamlet, they met a workman, and Tommy stopped him with a question."}, {"paragraph": 104, "text": ""The Moat House? It's empty. Been empty for years. Mrs. Sweeny's got the key if you want to go over it--next to the post office.""}, {"paragraph": 105, "text": "Mrs. Sweeny readily produced the key."}, {"paragraph": 106, "text": "Tommy asked, "You've not had a young lady here asking for this key to-day?""}, {"paragraph": 107, "text": "The woman shook her head."}, {"paragraph": 108, "text": ""No one's been over the place for a long time.""}, {"paragraph": 109, "text": "They retraced their steps to the Moat House. As the front door swung back, Julius struck a match and examined the floor carefully."}, {"paragraph": 110, "text": ""I'd swear no one's passed this way. Look at the dust. Thick. Not a sign of a footmark.""}, {"paragraph": 111, "text": ""This gets me," said Julius. "I don't believe Tuppence was ever in this house.""}, {"paragraph": 112, "text": ""She must have been," Tommy said. "We'll go over it again to-morrow.""}, {"paragraph": 113, "text": "On the morrow, as they were retracing their steps to the gate, Tommy gave a sudden cry, and stooping, picked something up from among the leaves. It was a small gold brooch."}, {"paragraph": 114, "text": ""That's Tuppence's!""}, {"paragraph": 115, "text": ""Are you sure?""}, {"paragraph": 116, "text": ""Absolutely. I've often seen her wear it.""}, {"paragraph": 117, "text": "Julius drew a deep breath."}, {"paragraph": 118, "text": ""I guess that settles it. She came as far as here, anyway. Somebody _must_ have seen her.""}, {"paragraph": 119, "text": "Forthwith the campaign began. Nobody answering to Tuppence's description had been seen in the vicinity."}, {"paragraph": 120, "text": "Julius wired to town for his own car, and they scoured the neighbourhood daily. Every car that had passed through the village on the fateful day was tracked down; but, as day succeeded day, they were no nearer to discovering Tuppence's whereabouts."}, {"paragraph": 121, "text": ""Do you know how long we've been here?" Tommy asked one morning at breakfast. "A week! We're no nearer to finding Tuppence, _and next Sunday is the_ 29_th!_""}, {"paragraph": 122, "text": ""Shucks!" said Julius thoughtfully. "I'd almost forgotten about the 29th.""}, {"paragraph": 123, "text": ""To-day's the 23rd, and time's getting short," Tommy said. "If we're ever going to get hold of her at all, we must do it before the 29th--her life won't be worth an hour's purchase afterwards. The hostage game will be played out by then.""}, {"paragraph": 124, "text": ""I'm with you there. We've been a couple of mutts. I'm going right back to London to put the case in the hands of your British police. Scotland Yard for me! Are you coming along with me?""}, {"paragraph": 125, "text": "Tommy shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 126, "text": ""One of us is enough. I might as well stay here and nose round a bit longer. Something _might_ turn up.""}, {"paragraph": 127, "text": ""Sure thing. Well, so long. I'll be back in a couple of shakes with a few inspectors along.""}, {"paragraph": 128, "text": "Later in the day Tommy received a wire:"}, {"paragraph": 129, "text": ""Join me Manchester Midland Hotel. Important news--JULIUS.""}, {"paragraph": 130, "text": "At 7.30 that night Tommy alighted from a slow cross-country train. Julius was on the platform."}, {"paragraph": 131, "text": ""What is it? Is Tuppence found?""}, {"paragraph": 132, "text": "Julius shook his head."}, {"paragraph": 133, "text": ""No. But I found this waiting in London. Just arrived.""}, {"paragraph": 134, "text": "He handed the telegraph form to the other. Tommy's eyes opened as he read:"}, {"paragraph": 135, "text": ""Jane Finn found. Come Manchester Midland Hotel immediately--PEEL EDGERTON.""}, {"paragraph": 136, "text": "Julius took the form back and folded it up."}, {"paragraph": 137, "text": ""Queer," he said thoughtfully. "I thought that lawyer chap had quit!""}], "026.source": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "HER arm through Jane’s, dragging her along, Tuppence reached the
station. Her quick ears caught the sound of the approaching train."}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "“Hurry up,” she panted, “or we’ll miss it.”"}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "They arrived on the platform just as the train came to a standstill.
Tuppence opened the door of an empty first-class compartment, and the
two girls sank down breathless on the padded seats."}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "A man looked in, then passed on to the next carriage. Jane started
nervously. Her eyes dilated with terror. She looked questioningly at
Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "“Is he one of them, do you think?” she breathed."}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "Tuppence shook her head."}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "“No, no. It’s all right.” She took Jane’s hand in hers. “Tommy wouldn’t
have told us to do this unless he was sure we’d be all right.”"}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "“But he doesn’t know them as I do!” The girl shivered. “You can’t
understand. Five years! Five long years! Sometimes I thought I should go
mad.”"}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“Never mind. It’s all over.”"}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "“Is it?”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "The train was moving now, speeding through the night at a gradually
increasing rate. Suddenly Jane Finn started up."}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“What was that? I thought I saw a face--looking in through the window.”"}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "“No, there’s nothing. See.” Tuppence went to the window, and lifting the
strap let the pane down."}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“You’re sure?”"}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "“Quite sure.”"}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "The other seemed to feel some excuse was necessary:"}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“I guess I’m acting like a frightened rabbit, but I can’t help it. If
they caught me now they’d----” Her eyes opened wide and staring."}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“_Don’t!_” implored Tuppence. “Lie back, and _don’t think_. You can be
quite sure that Tommy wouldn’t have said it was safe if it wasn’t.”"}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“My cousin didn’t think so. He didn’t want us to do this.”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "“No,” said Tuppence, rather embarrassed."}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“What are you thinking of?” said Jane sharply."}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "“Why?”"}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“Your voice was so--queer!”"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "“I _was_ thinking of something,” confessed Tuppence. “But I don’t want
to tell you--not now. I may be wrong, but I don’t think so. It’s just
an idea that came into my head a long time ago. Tommy’s got it too--I’m
almost sure he has. But don’t _you_ worry--there’ll be time enough for
that later. And it mayn’t be so at all! Do what I tell you--lie back and
don’t think of anything.”"}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "“I’ll try.” The long lashes drooped over the hazel eyes."}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "Tuppence, for her part, sat bolt upright--much in the attitude of a
watchful terrier on guard. In spite of herself she was nervous. Her eyes
flashed continually from one window to the other. She noted the exact
position of the communication cord. What it was that she feared, she
would have been hard put to it to say. But in her own mind she was
far from feeling the confidence displayed in her words. Not that she
disbelieved in Tommy, but occasionally she was shaken with doubts as to
whether anyone so simple and honest as he was could ever be a match for
the fiendish subtlety of the arch-criminal."}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "If they once reached Sir James Peel Edgerton in safety, all would be
well. But would they reach him? Would not the silent forces of Mr. Brown
already be assembling against them? Even that last picture of Tommy,
revolver in hand, failed to comfort her. By now he might be overpowered,
borne down by sheer force of numbers.... Tuppence mapped out her plan of
campaign."}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "As the train at length drew slowly into Charing Cross, Jane Finn sat up
with a start."}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "“Have we arrived? I never thought we should!”"}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“Oh, I thought we’d get to London all right. If there’s going to be any
fun, now is when it will begin. Quick, get out. We’ll nip into a taxi.”"}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "In another minute they were passing the barrier, had paid the necessary
fares, and were stepping into a taxi."}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“King’s Cross,” directed Tuppence. Then she gave a jump. A man looked in
at the window, just as they started. She was almost certain it was the
same man who had got into the carriage next to them. She had a horrible
feeling of being slowly hemmed in on every side."}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“You see,” she explained to Jane, “if they think we’re going to Sir
James, this will put them off the scent. Now they’ll imagine we’re going
to Mr. Carter. His country place is north of London somewhere.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "Crossing Holborn there was a block, and the taxi was held up. This was
what Tuppence had been waiting for."}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“Quick,” she whispered. “Open the right-hand door!”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "The two girls stepped out into the traffic. Two minutes later they were
seated in another taxi and were retracing their steps, this time direct
to Carlton House Terrace."}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“There,” said Tuppence, with great satisfaction, “this ought to do them.
I can’t help thinking that I’m really rather clever! How that other taxi
man will swear! But I took his number, and I’ll send him a postal order
to-morrow, so that he won’t lose by it if he happens to be genuine.
What’s this thing swerving----Oh!”"}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "There was a grinding noise and a bump. Another taxi had collided with
them."}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "In a flash Tuppence was out on the pavement. A policeman was
approaching. Before he arrived Tuppence had handed the driver five
shillings, and she and Jane had merged themselves in the crowd."}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“It’s only a step or two now,” said Tuppence breathlessly. The accident
had taken place in Trafalgar Square."}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "“Do you think the collision was an accident, or done deliberately?”"}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“I don’t know. It might have been either.”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "Hand-in-hand, the two girls hurried along."}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "“It may be my fancy,” said Tuppence suddenly, “but I feel as though
there was some one behind us.”"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“Hurry!” murmured the other. “Oh, hurry!”"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "They were now at the corner of Carlton House Terrace, and their spirits
lightened. Suddenly a large and apparently intoxicated man barred their
way."}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "“Good evening, ladies,” he hiccupped. “Whither away so fast?”"}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“Let us pass, please,” said Tuppence imperiously."}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "“Just a word with your pretty friend here.” He stretched out an unsteady
hand, and clutched Jane by the shoulder. Tuppence heard other footsteps
behind. She did not pause to ascertain whether they were friends or
foes. Lowering her head, she repeated a manœuvre of childish days,
and butted their aggressor full in the capacious middle. The success of
these unsportsmanlike tactics was immediate. The man sat down abruptly
on the pavement. Tuppence and Jane took to their heels. The house they
sought was some way down. Other footsteps echoed behind them. Their
breath was coming in choking gasps as they reached Sir James’s door.
Tuppence seized the bell and Jane the knocker."}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "The man who had stopped them reached the foot of the steps. For a moment
he hesitated, and as he did so the door opened. They fell into the hall
together. Sir James came forward from the library door."}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“Hullo! What’s this?”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "He stepped forward, and put his arm round Jane as she swayed
uncertainly. He half carried her into the library, and laid her on the
leather couch. From a tantalus on the table he poured out a few drops of
brandy, and forced her to drink them. With a sigh she sat up, her eyes
still wild and frightened."}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“It’s all right. Don’t be afraid, my child. You’re quite safe.”"}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "Her breath came more normally, and the colour was returning to her
cheeks. Sir James looked at Tuppence quizzically."}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“So you’re not dead, Miss Tuppence, any more than that Tommy boy of
yours was!”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "“The Young Adventurers take a lot of killing,” boasted Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“So it seems,” said Sir James dryly. “Am I right in thinking that the
joint venture has ended in success, and that this”--he turned to the
girl on the couch--“is Miss Jane Finn?”"}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "Jane sat up."}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“Yes,” she said quietly, “I am Jane Finn. I have a lot to tell you.”"}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "“When you are stronger----”"}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“No--now!” Her voice rose a little. “I shall feel safer when I have told
everything.”"}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“As you please,” said the lawyer."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "He sat down in one of the big arm-chairs facing the couch. In a low
voice Jane began her story."}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "“I came over on the _Lusitania_ to take up a post in Paris. I was
fearfully keen about the war, and just dying to help somehow or other. I
had been studying French, and my teacher said they were wanting help in
a hospital in Paris, so I wrote and offered my services, and they were
accepted. I hadn’t got any folk of my own, so it made it easy to arrange
things."}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "“When the _Lusitania_ was torpedoed, a man came up to me. I’d noticed
him more than once--and I’d figured it out in my own mind that he
was afraid of somebody or something. He asked me if I was a patriotic
American, and told me he was carrying papers which were just life or
death to the Allies. He asked me to take charge of them. I was to watch
for an advertisement in the _Times_. If it didn’t appear, I was to take
them to the American Ambassador."}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "“Most of what followed seems like a nightmare still. I see it in my
dreams sometimes.... I’ll hurry over that part. Mr. Danvers had told me
to watch out. He might have been shadowed from New York, but he didn’t
think so. At first I had no suspicions, but on the boat to Holyhead I
began to get uneasy. There was one woman who had been very keen to look
after me, and chum up with me generally--a Mrs. Vandemeyer. At first I’d
been only grateful to her for being so kind to me; but all the time I
felt there was something about her I didn’t like, and on the Irish
boat I saw her talking to some queer-looking men, and from the way they
looked I saw that they were talking about me. I remembered that she’d
been quite near me on the _Lusitania_ when Mr. Danvers gave me the
packet, and before that she’d tried to talk to him once or twice. I
began to get scared, but I didn’t quite see what to do."}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“I had a wild idea of stopping at Holyhead, and not going on to London
that day, but I soon saw that that would be plumb foolishness. The only
thing was to act as though I’d noticed nothing, and hope for the best.
I couldn’t see how they could get me if I was on my guard. One thing
I’d done already as a precaution--ripped open the oilskin packet and
substituted blank paper, and then sewn it up again. So, if anyone did
manage to rob me of it, it wouldn’t matter."}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "“What to do with the real thing worried me no end. Finally I opened it
out flat--there were only two sheets--and laid it between two of the
advertisement pages of a magazine. I stuck the two pages together
round the edge with some gum off an envelope. I carried the magazine
carelessly stuffed into the pocket of my ulster."}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "“At Holyhead I tried to get into a carriage with people that looked all
right, but in a queer way there seemed always to be a crowd round me
shoving and pushing me just the way I didn’t want to go. There was
something uncanny and frightening about it. In the end I found myself in
a carriage with Mrs. Vandemeyer after all. I went out into the corridor,
but all the other carriages were full, so I had to go back and sit down.
I consoled myself with the thought that there were other people in the
carriage--there was quite a nice-looking man and his wife sitting just
opposite. So I felt almost happy about it until just outside London. I
had leaned back and closed my eyes. I guess they thought I was asleep,
but my eyes weren’t quite shut, and suddenly I saw the nice-looking man
get something out of his bag and hand it to Mrs. Vandemeyer, and as he
did so he _winked_...."}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“I can’t tell you how that wink sort of froze me through and through. My
only thought was to get out in the corridor as quick as ever I could. I
got up, trying to look natural and easy. Perhaps they saw something--I
don’t know--but suddenly Mrs. Vandemeyer said ‘Now,’ and flung something
over my nose and mouth as I tried to scream. At the same moment I felt a
terrific blow on the back of my head....”"}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "She shuddered. Sir James murmured something sympathetically. In a minute
she resumed:"}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“I don’t know how long it was before I came back to consciousness. I
felt very ill and sick. I was lying on a dirty bed. There was a
screen round it, but I could hear two people talking in the room. Mrs.
Vandemeyer was one of them. I tried to listen, but at first I couldn’t
take much in. When at last I did begin to grasp what was going on--I was
just terrified! I wonder I didn’t scream right out there and then."}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "“They hadn’t found the papers. They’d got the oilskin packet with the
blanks, and they were just mad! They didn’t know whether _I_‘d changed
the papers, or whether Danvers had been carrying a dummy message,
while the real one was sent another way. They spoke of”--she closed her
eyes--“torturing me to find out!"}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“I’d never known what fear--really sickening fear--was before! Once
they came to look at me. I shut my eyes and pretended to be still
unconscious, but I was afraid they’d hear the beating of my heart.
However, they went away again. I began thinking madly. What could I do?
I knew I wouldn’t be able to stand up against torture very long."}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“Suddenly something put the thought of loss of memory into my head. The
subject had always interested me, and I’d read an awful lot about it.
I had the whole thing at my finger-tips. If only I could succeed in
carrying the bluff through, it might save me. I said a prayer, and drew
a long breath. Then I opened my eyes and started babbling in _French!_"}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“Mrs. Vandemeyer came round the screen at once. Her face was so wicked I
nearly died, but I smiled up at her doubtfully, and asked her in French
where I was."}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "“It puzzled her, I could see. She called the man she had been talking
to. He stood by the screen with his face in shadow. He spoke to me in
French. His voice was very ordinary and quiet, but somehow, I don’t know
why, he scared me worse than the woman. I felt he’d seen right through
me, but I went on playing my part. I asked again where I was, and
then went on that there was something I _must_ remember--_must_
remember--only for the moment it was all gone. I worked myself up to
be more and more distressed. He asked me my name. I said I didn’t
know--that I couldn’t remember anything at all."}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "“Suddenly he caught my wrist, and began twisting it. The pain was awful.
I screamed. He went on. I screamed and screamed, but I managed to shriek
out things in French. I don’t know how long I could have gone on, but
luckily I fainted. The last thing I heard was his voice saying: ‘That’s
not bluff! Anyway, a kid of her age wouldn’t know enough.’ I guess he
forgot American girls are older for their age than English ones, and
take more interest in scientific subjects."}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“When I came to, Mrs. Vandemeyer was sweet as honey to me. She’d had her
orders, I guess. She spoke to me in French--told me I’d had a shock
and been very ill. I should be better soon. I pretended to be rather
dazed--murmured something about the ‘doctor’ having hurt my wrist. She
looked relieved when I said that."}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "“By and by she went out of the room altogether. I was suspicious still,
and lay quite quiet for some time. In the end, however, I got up and
walked round the room, examining it. I thought that even if anyone
_was_ watching me from somewhere, it would seem natural enough under
the circumstances. It was a squalid, dirty place. There were no windows,
which seemed queer. I guessed the door would be locked, but I didn’t
try it. There were some battered old pictures on the walls, representing
scenes from _Faust_.”"}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "Jane’s two listeners gave a simultaneous “Ah!” The girl nodded."}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“Yes--it was the place in Soho where Mr. Beresford was imprisoned. Of
course, at the time I didn’t even know if I was in London. One thing was
worrying me dreadfully, but my heart gave a great throb of relief when
I saw my ulster lying carelessly over the back of a chair. _And the
magazine was still rolled up in the pocket!_"}, {"paragraph": 83, "text": "“If only I could be certain that I was not being overlooked! I looked
carefully round the walls. There didn’t seem to be a peep-hole of any
kind--nevertheless I felt kind of sure there must be. All of a sudden I
sat down on the edge of the table, and put my face in my hands, sobbing
out a ‘Mon Dieu! Mon Dieu!’ I’ve got very sharp ears. I distinctly heard
the rustle of a dress, and slight creak. That was enough for me. I was
being watched!"}, {"paragraph": 84, "text": "“I lay down on the bed again, and by and by Mrs. Vandemeyer brought me
some supper. She was still sweet as they make them. I guess she’d been
told to win my confidence. Presently she produced the oilskin packet,
and asked me if I recognized it, watching me like a lynx all the time."}, {"paragraph": 85, "text": "“I took it and turned it over in a puzzled sort of way. Then I shook my
head. I said that I felt I _ought_ to remember something about it, that
it was just as though it was all coming back, and then, before I could
get hold of it, it went again. Then she told me that I was her niece,
and that I was to call her ‘Aunt Rita.’ I did obediently, and she told
me not to worry--my memory would soon come back."}, {"paragraph": 86, "text": "“That was an awful night. I’d made my plan whilst I was waiting for her.
The papers were safe so far, but I couldn’t take the risk of leaving
them there any longer. They might throw that magazine away any minute.
I lay awake waiting until I judged it must be about two o’clock in the
morning. Then I got up as softly as I could, and felt in the dark along
the left-hand wall. Very gently, I unhooked one of the pictures from its
nail--Marguerite with her casket of jewels. I crept over to my coat and
took out the magazine, and an odd envelope or two that I had shoved in.
Then I went to the washstand, and damped the brown paper at the back
of the picture all round. Presently I was able to pull it away. I had
already torn out the two stuck-together pages from the magazine, and now
I slipped them with their precious enclosure between the picture and its
brown paper backing. A little gum from the envelopes helped me to
stick the latter up again. No one would dream the picture had ever been
tampered with. I rehung it on the wall, put the magazine back in my
coat pocket, and crept back to bed. I was pleased with my hiding-place.
They’d never think of pulling to pieces one of their own pictures. I
hoped that they’d come to the conclusion that Danvers had been carrying
a dummy all along, and that, in the end, they’d let me go."}, {"paragraph": 87, "text": "“As a matter of fact, I guess that’s what they did think at first, and,
in a way, it was dangerous for me. I learnt afterwards that they nearly
did away with me then and there--there was never much chance of their
‘letting me go’--but the first man, who was the boss, preferred to keep
me alive on the chance of my having hidden them, and being able to tell
where if I recovered my memory. They watched me constantly for weeks.
Sometimes they’d ask me questions by the hour--I guess there was nothing
they didn’t know about the third degree!--but somehow I managed to hold
my own. The strain of it was awful, though...."}, {"paragraph": 88, "text": "“They took me back to Ireland, and over every step of the journey again,
in case I’d hidden it somewhere _en route_. Mrs. Vandemeyer and another
woman never left me for a moment. They spoke of me as a young relative
of Mrs. Vandemeyer’s whose mind was affected by the shock of the
_Lusitania_. There was no one I could appeal to for help without
giving myself away to _them_, and if I risked it and failed--and Mrs.
Vandemeyer looked so rich, and so beautifully dressed, that I felt
convinced they’d take her word against mine, and think it was part of my
mental trouble to think myself ‘persecuted’--I felt that the horrors in
store for me would be too awful once they knew I’d been only shamming.”"}, {"paragraph": 89, "text": "Sir James nodded comprehendingly."}, {"paragraph": 90, "text": "“Mrs. Vandemeyer was a woman of great personality. With that and her
social position she would have had little difficulty in imposing her
point of view in preference to yours. Your sensational accusations
against her would not easily have found credence.”"}, {"paragraph": 91, "text": "“That’s what I thought. It ended in my being sent to a sanatorium at
Bournemouth. I couldn’t make up my mind at first whether it was a sham
affair or genuine. A hospital nurse had charge of me. I was a special
patient. She seemed so nice and normal that at last I determined to
confide in her. A merciful providence just saved me in time from falling
into the trap. My door happened to be ajar, and I heard her talking to
some one in the passage. _She was one of them!_ They still fancied it
might be a bluff on my part, and she was put in charge of me to make
sure! After that, my nerve went completely. I dared trust nobody."}, {"paragraph": 92, "text": "“I think I almost hypnotized myself. After a while, I almost forgot
that I was really Jane Finn. I was so bent on playing the part of Janet
Vandemeyer that my nerves began to play me tricks. I became really
ill--for months I sank into a sort of stupor. I felt sure I should
die soon, and that nothing really mattered. A sane person shut up in a
lunatic asylum often ends by becoming insane, they say. I guess I was
like that. Playing my part had become second nature to me. I wasn’t even
unhappy in the end--just apathetic. Nothing seemed to matter. And the
years went on."}, {"paragraph": 93, "text": "“And then suddenly things seemed to change. Mrs. Vandemeyer came down
from London. She and the doctor asked me questions, experimented with
various treatments. There was some talk of sending me to a specialist in
Paris. In the end, they did not dare risk it. I overheard something that
seemed to show that other people--friends--were looking for me. I
learnt later that the nurse who had looked after me went to Paris,
and consulted a specialist, representing herself to be me. He put her
through some searching tests, and exposed her loss of memory to be
fraudulent; but she had taken a note of his methods and reproduced
them on me. I dare say I couldn’t have deceived the specialist for a
minute--a man who has made a lifelong study of a thing is unique--but
I managed once again to hold my own with them. The fact that I’d not
thought of myself as Jane Finn for so long made it easier."}, {"paragraph": 94, "text": "“One night I was whisked off to London at a moment’s notice. They took
me back to the house in Soho. Once I got away from the sanatorium I felt
different--as though something in me that had been buried for a long
time was waking up again."}, {"paragraph": 95, "text": "“They sent me in to wait on Mr. Beresford. (Of course I didn’t know
his name then.) I was suspicious--I thought it was another trap. But he
looked so honest, I could hardly believe it. However, I was careful in
all I said, for I knew we could be overheard. There’s a small hole, high
